title: Memory Palace Challenge
shortDescription: A method-of-loci memory exercise — place items along an imagined route, then recall them in order.
longDescription: Memory Palace Challenge is built on the Method of Loci ("memory palace") — the oldest documented memory technique, traced to ancient Greek and Roman rhetoric, and still the core technique behind competitive memory-sport disciplines like the World Memory Championships' serial-recall events. You study a route of locations, each holding one item, then recall the items in the exact order they appeared along the route. Recall is scored by strict serial position — an item remembered but placed in the wrong slot doesn't count, matching how serial recall is scored in memory research.
sourceNote: The Method of Loci is a technique, not a single copyrighted test, so there's no proprietary instrument being adapted here — these four routes and their items are original content built to implement the technique faithfully. Ordered recall is scored via the `sequence` question type, which stores each item's correct 1-indexed route position in its `value` field and credits it only when placed in that exact position (src/lib/scoring/engine.ts) — previously this question type wasn't scored at all; that gap is fixed as of this assessment. Each round also includes two position-probe questions ("what was at stop 3?"), a genuine supplementary measure used alongside full serial recall in memory research, not padding.

sections.name: Route 1: Home
sections.instructions: Study this route, in order: 1. Front Door → Umbrella · 2. Hallway → Painting · 3. Kitchen → Teapot · 4. Living Room → Lamp · 5. Bedroom → Alarm Clock. Picture yourself walking the route, seeing each item at its stop.

sections.name: Route 2: Cottage Garden
sections.description: A 6-stop route through a garden and cottage.
sections.instructions: Study this route, in order: 1. Garden Gate → Watering Can · 2. Porch → Welcome Mat · 3. Foyer → Mirror · 4. Staircase → Candle · 5. Study → Globe · 6. Attic → Trunk.

sections.name: Route 3: Office Building
sections.description: A 7-stop route through an office building.
sections.instructions: Study this route, in order: 1. Lobby → Fountain · 2. Elevator → Plant · 3. Office Floor → Whiteboard · 4. Break Room → Coffee Pot · 5. Conference Room → Projector · 6. Supply Closet → Stapler · 7. Rooftop → Antenna.

sections.name: Route 4: Mountain Trail
sections.description: An 8-stop route along a hiking trail.
sections.instructions: Study this route, in order: 1. Trailhead → Compass · 2. Bridge → Rope · 3. Meadow → Canteen · 4. Forest Edge → Lantern · 5. Cave Mouth → Torch · 6. River Bend → Fishing Rod · 7. Campsite → Tent · 8. Summit → Flag.

scoringDimensions.label: Memory Palace Recall
scoringDimensions.description: Composite score across ordered recall and position-probe accuracy.

scoringDimensions.label: Ordered Recall
scoringDimensions.description: Recalling the full route's items in exact serial order.

scoringDimensions.label: Position Accuracy
scoringDimensions.description: Correctly identifying what was at a specific stop.

resultRanges.title: Developing
resultRanges.description: Ordered recall across a full route is difficult right now — the technique itself takes practice before the palace "sticks."
recommendations: Start with shorter routes (3-4 stops) and build up gradually
Make the mental images vivid and slightly absurd — bizarre images are easier to recall than plain ones
Walk the route in your head at least twice before attempting recall

resultRanges.title: Average
resultRanges.description: Shorter routes are manageable, but longer ones or a route studied only once lose items partway through.
recommendations: Practice the same route repeatedly until the order feels automatic before moving to a new one
Use real, familiar locations (your actual home) instead of generic ones — familiarity anchors the route

resultRanges.title: Strong
resultRanges.description: Reliable ordered recall across most routes, with occasional slips on the longer ones.
recommendations: Push route length further — competitive memory athletes use routes with dozens of stops
Practice recalling routes out of order (e.g. "what was at stop 5?") to strengthen the underlying spatial map, not just the sequence

resultRanges.title: Very Strong
resultRanges.description: Consistently accurate ordered recall even on the longest route, with strong position accuracy too.
recommendations: This technique scales well — try applying it to real material you need to memorize (a speech, a list, key facts)
Build multiple palaces for different topics so they don't interfere with each other

resultRanges.title: Exceptional
resultRanges.description: Near-perfect ordered recall across every route — the core skill behind competitive memory-sport performance.
recommendations: This is genuinely competition-level serial recall — the World Memory Championships' disciplines use the same core technique at larger scale
Consider extending routes further, or memorizing genuinely long real-world sequences
